Why different hazards need different evidence

Landslides, snow avalanches and vegetation fires can affect some of the same assets, including roads, settlements and natural ecosystems. Their management differs because the underlying physical processes are not the same. A landslide assessment concentrates on slope stability and earth materials. An avalanche assessment concentrates on snowpack stability and the possible movement of snow. A fire assessment considers ignition, combustible vegetation and the conditions governing flame spread.

For objective questions, it is useful to connect each hazard to its major triggers, the information required for warning and the institution most closely associated with the relevant national scientific work.

AspectLandslideSnow avalancheForest or grassland fire
Material or processMoving rock, soil or debrisMoving snow, sometimes with debrisCombustion of vegetation
Important triggers or conditionsRainfall, groundwater change, shaking and slope disturbanceUnstable snow layers, heavy snowfall, wind loading and warmingIgnition, dry fuel, wind and favourable terrain
Important assessmentSusceptibility, movement and rainfallSnowpack stability and avalanche pathsFire danger, fuel and thermal hotspots
National scientific organisationGSIDGRE under DRDOFSI
Major preventive emphasisSafe land use, slope assessment and drainageAvoiding hazardous snow slopes and runout zonesIgnition prevention, fuel management and early detection

These institutional associations identify important specialist responsibilities; they do not mean that a single agency manages every aspect of a disaster. Local administrations, State Disaster Management Authorities, District Disaster Management Authorities and relevant operational agencies coordinate action according to the situation.

Three distinctions that prevent common errors

Susceptibility is not an immediate warning

A region may be susceptible to landslides for many years without experiencing movement on a particular day. Likewise, a fire-danger rating describes conditions favourable to fire and does not establish that flames have already appeared. An avalanche-prone route may remain exposed even during a period without active snowfall.

Detection is not the same as complete measurement

A forest-fire hotspot is evidence of a thermal anomaly detected by a satellite. It is not automatically one separate fire incident or a direct measurement of total burned area. Similarly, a reported crack or small slope movement may justify investigation but does not by itself establish the exact size or timing of a future landslide.

Protective measures reduce risk but rarely remove it entirely

Drainage and vegetation can improve some slopes, but neither prevents every landslide. Avoiding avalanche paths reduces exposure, but snowfall and changing conditions can create uncertainty. Fire lines may interrupt surface fuel but do not always stop wind-driven embers. Good management combines prevention, monitoring, public communication and appropriate response.

Applying the ideas to public safety

The safest general public response to a serious warning is to avoid entering the threatened area, follow instructions from responsible authorities and report observed danger without approaching it. Returning to an area should depend on official safety information rather than assuming that the hazard has ended because rain, snowfall or visible flames have stopped.

Prelims focus

  • GSI: landslide studies, susceptibility mapping and landslide-related forecasting.
  • DGRE under DRDO: snow-avalanche research and warnings.
  • FSI: forest-fire danger information and satellite-based alerts.
  • Rainfall-induced landslides, unstable snow avalanches and wind-driven vegetation fires involve different physical mechanisms.
  • Public protection depends on reducing exposure and following applicable official warnings.
  • Trap: Risk maps, danger ratings, hotspot detections and actual disaster incidents are not interchangeable measures.

[Sources: NDMA, Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches, June 2009, chapters 1–2 and sections on mitigation and warning; GSI, National Landslide Forecasting Centre, official institutional information, consulted 2 November 2026; DRDO, Natural Hazard Management, section Avalanche Early Warning, consulted 2 November 2026; FSI, Near Real-Time Forest Fire Monitoring and Pre-Fire Alert Based on Forest Fire Danger Rating, consulted 2 November 2026; MoEFCC, National Action Plan on Forest Fire, April 2018.]
